newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Act, govt reach understanding on committees.
newsitem.headline: NZ Act, govt reach understanding on committees.

text.p: Act New Zealand deputy leader Ken Shirley said on Thursday that Act had reached "an understanding" with the government over the make-up of parliamentary select committees.

"We have reached a political understanding. The select committees elect their own chair. We cannot pre-empt that, but... around parliament people talk to each other... and come to understandings," Shirley told Reuters in an interview.

The formation of the committees has been delayed by a row over how many committees the main opposition Labour Party will chair. Unless agreement is reached they will be set up by parliament in the first weeks of March.

The committees, which examine proposed legislation, review departmental funding and have the power to initiate inquiries, normally have eight members and are set up to reflect the make- up of parliament.

But Shirley said that did not imply the chairs should be proportionally distributed as Labour had argued. He said as part of the understanding with the government, Act would chair one of the committees.
He would not say who, or which committee.
Shirley said Act would have nine members on the 12 business committees and expected to win all the places it sought.
The governing National-New Zealand First coalition has 61 seats in the 120-member pariament and would have difficulty installing its chairpersons without an understanding with Act's eight MPs.
The committees have already breached the timetable for their statutory examination of reports from government departments.

Shirley said it was a "constitutional outrage" that the committees had taken so long to be set up. He blamed the length of the coalition talks after the October 12 election and the failure to call the House earlier than February 18 for the delay.
He was also critical of Labour for refusing permission for parliament's business committee to set up the committees.
"You could argue parliament was not properly constituted until the committees were up and running. We have effectively lost four to six months of time," he said.
